subtopics.title: Carbon allotropes and property differences

slots.X: A schematic carbon fragment A has eight vertices; six have three bonded neighbours and two have two. Fragment B has six vertices; four have four neighbours and two have two. Calculate distinct links for each, then explain whether either count proves a complete graphite or diamond lattice. Sketch a local three-neighbour planar arrangement and a four-neighbour spatial arrangement; show why boundary vertices invalidate the periodic count rule.
slots.Y: Coordination is the number of nearest bonded neighbours, not bond order or isolated bond strength. In an ideal periodic network each link is shared by two atoms; graphite has delocalised electrons in layers.
slots.Z: A degree sum 6×3+2×2=22, 11 links; B=4×4+2×2=20, 10 links. Counts alone do not establish allotrope: boundary coordination, geometry and electronic structure matter. Graphite local trigonal planar arrangement, diamond local tetrahedral arrangement; edge vertices have lower coordination so uniform periodic degree assumption fails. Link count does not measure bond strength.
slots.W: Translate nonuniform coordination into link counts and distinguish local geometry from global lattice identity.

slots.X: A carbon laminate is electrically measured in two directions. Rotating the sample by 90° relative to fixed electrodes exchanges the high and low readings; replacing the electrodes with different contacts changes both readings similarly. Cleavage is easy along visible planes. Combine the evidence to distinguish orientation-dependent material transport from contact resistance alone, and specify an independent measurement that would challenge the layered model.
slots.Y: Structure–property reasoning may involve geometry, carrier paths, interlayer interaction and contact effects. A change in a single reading does not establish a phase transition or unique material identity.
slots.Z: Rotation-dependent exchange tracks the sample axes and supports intrinsic anisotropy, whereas common shifts with changed contacts indicate measurement contribution. Easy cleavage along planes supports layered structure. A contact-only hypothesis may still involve orientation-dependent contact geometry; control geometry and use four-probe direction-resolved measurement and structural diffraction. Neither reading proves composition or unique allotrope.
slots.W: Combine rotated-sample and changed-contact evidence to distinguish competing causes.

slots.X: Equal-mass elemental carbon samples P and Q have same isotopic composition. P conducts along layers and cleaves easily; Q resists scratching and ordinarily does not conduct. slots.Y: Allotropes are distinct structures of one element. Graphite has strong in-plane bonding and weaker interlayer interactions; diamond forms a three-dimensional network. Hardness, transport and atom count are different observables, affected by defects and orientation.

subtopics.title: Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons

slots.X: Two proposed connected hydrocarbons have six carbons. A is acyclic with two C=C bonds; B has one ring and one C≡C bond. A student labels both C₆H₁₀. Construct valid explicit examples, count hydrogens from bond orders, correct the labels, and decide whether ideal multiple-bond hydrogenation (rings unchanged) makes the products have equal formulas.
slots.Y: For typical neutral connected hydrocarbons, a ring or double bond reduces hydrogen count by two relative to acyclic saturation; triple reduces by four. Hydrogen-deficiency formula is extension context; formula alone does not identify structure.
slots.Z: A: hexa-1,3-diene CH₂=CH–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃, C₆H₁₀. B: ethynylcyclobutane, C₄H₇–C≡CH, C₆H₈; the ring contributes one deficit and triple two. A adds 2H₂→C₆H₁₄; B adds 2H₂→C₆H₁₂ (ring remains), under stated model. Not equal. Check carbon valence and H counts: B has one ring CH, three ring CH₂ and one terminal alkyne H.
slots.W: Translate structural constraints to two valid graphs and compare independent atom counts before and after reaction.

slots.X: An unknown pure C₄H₆ hydrocarbon consumes exactly 2 mol H₂ per mole in an ideal complete catalytic hydrogenation that changes only multiple bonds and leaves all rings intact. The final product is acyclic C₄H₁₀. Combine hydrogen deficiency and reaction evidence, draw two starting structures compatible with both, and identify one measurement that would distinguish them.

slots.Z: C₄H₆ has two deficiency units relative to C₄H₁₀. Two H₂ add four H; final acyclic so initial no ring under model. But-1-yne HC≡C–CH₂–CH₃ and buta-1,3-diene CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ both meet total uptake and yield butane. Distinguish via suitable structural spectroscopy or bond-specific evidence. Hydrogen uptake alone does not choose triple vs two doubles.
slots.W: Combine formula and selective reaction constraints; construct distinct compatible structures.

subtopics.title: Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents

slots.X: Two ideal surfactant sketches show (A) heads at the water-facing surface and tails toward an oil droplet, (B) heads buried in oil and tails facing water. Represent both with labelled water/oil regions and explain which orientation supports an oil-in-water dispersion. Predict what changes when calcium binds the soap heads.
slots.Y: Amphiphilic molecules contain hydrophobic tails and hydrophilic heads; aggregate geometry depends on surrounding phases. Divalent ions can remove soap through precipitation, distinct from micellisation.
slots.Z: A is compatible with aqueous dispersion: hydrophobic tails associate with oil, ionic hydrophilic heads contact water. B reversed orientation is not typical oil-in-water arrangement. Ca²⁺ can form sparingly soluble carboxylate salt, reducing available active soap; not every remaining aggregate behaves identically. Foam not a direct measure of removal.
slots.W: Construct labelled molecular orientation and connect changed head chemistry to dispersion.

Infer A's Mg²⁺ amount, decide whether B removes all hardness, and propose a discriminating measurement if foam heights happen to match.

Matched foam does not establish equal residual hardness; independently measure residual ions/free surfactant under controlled conditions.

slots.X: Two pure liquids are ethanol and ethanoic acid. In ideal separate tests an equal 0.050 mol portion of each is contacted with excess hydrogen carbonate; one generates 0.050 mol CO₂ and the other none. Equal portions are then combined in a theoretical 1:1 esterification with 60% conversion. Justify identification, calculate ester/water and remaining reactants, and explain why the initial gas observation does not establish a real mixture's purity.
slots.Y: Carboxylic acid can transfer proton to hydrogen carbonate. Esterification is reversible; conversion controls product amount. Distinguish functional-group evidence from purity and theoretical yield.
slots.Z: Acid + HCO₃⁻→CH₃COO⁻+CO₂+H₂O; ethanoic acid gives .050 mol CO₂, ethanol no analogous response. CH₃COOH+C₂H₅OH⇌CH₃COOC₂H₅+H₂O. .030 mol ester and water; .020 mol acid and ethanol remain. Gas identifies acidic behaviour within pure candidates, not arbitrary mixtures. Separate portions, no practical instructions.
slots.W: Justify identification and cross-check reaction amounts under stated conversion and purity assumptions.
